paper_title: Efficient Ensemble for Fine-tuning Language Models on Multiple Datasets
caption: Illustrating the empirical generalization errors and sharpness measures with respect to QLoRA weights. (<ref>) Smaller adapters with a rank of 16 achieve the lowest generalization errors. Additionally, the Hessian trace values correlate with generalization errors, suggesting that smaller adapters tend to converge to flatter minima. (<ref>) An ensemble of k adapters leads to lower generalization errors and Hessian traces. Here, we fix the sum of the dimensions of k adapters to be equal to 256. (<ref>) QLoRA, which is trained on a quantized base model, yields lower generalization errors and Hessian trace values compared to LoRA.
model_annotation: The figure is a grouped vertical bar chart illustrating a quantity labeled as “Traces × 10−5 (RTE)” for two methods (LoRA and QLoRA) across several adapter ranks. The horizontal category axis is labeled “Rank” and shows four categories ordered left-to-right as 4, 16, 64, and 256. The vertical value axis corresponds to “Traces × 10−5 (RTE)” and uses a linear scale with labeled ticks at approximately 0.0, 3.0, and 6.0 (covering roughly 0 to a bit above 6). For each rank, two adjacent bars are shown: a blue bar for LoRA and an orange bar for QLoRA, each with a black capped error bar. At rank 4, the LoRA (blue) bar is near about 1.8–2.0 and the QLoRA (orange) bar is near about 1.7–1.9; at rank 16, LoRA is around 2.3–2.5 while QLoRA is around 0.7–0.9; at rank 64, LoRA is around 2.7–2.9 while QLoRA is around 0.9–1.1; at rank 256, LoRA is around 5.4–5.7 while QLoRA is around 3.5–3.7. The bars are grouped by rank with consistent side-by-side placement (LoRA on the left and QLoRA on the right within each group), and a legend identifying LoRA and QLoRA appears near the upper center of the plotting area; no bars appear specially emphasized beyond the standard coloring and error bars.
